idiom_name: destructuring exchange with typed bindings ([a, b] = [b, a])
implementation_notes: TypeScript compiles the same destructuring assignment as JavaScript (ES2015 target, or a temporary when downlevelled to ES5), so the language's exchange is [a, b] = [b, a] and the C++ structure has no analogue; the type system adds the constraints that make it safe - both sides must be assignable to the declared types, and readonly properties, readonly arrays and getter-only accessors refuse the assignment at compile time. The replacing shape is a single mutable state reference: model the representation as one property or one let binding and rebind it, keeping the fallible construction before the assignment and the rollback as the reverse assignment. Type declarations disappear at runtime, so the guarantee remains "one rebinding, no user code".
pitfalls: readonly properties, readonly arrays and as const values make the exchange a compile error - the type is immutable by design, so publish a new value instead of swapping parts (the readonly modifier is compile-time only and aliases can still mutate the underlying object).
Accessors (get/set) are ordinary methods: assigning through them runs user code and can throw, and a two-property swap is not atomic - only rebinding one private field is a commit you can rely on.
Type annotations do not survive to runtime, so an untyped or any-typed handle can hold a wrong-shaped state and the swap just moves the bug; keep the state type precise so commit() is checked.

Destructuring allocates a temporary array per exchange and ES5 downlevelling emits a longer temporary sequence; use a temporary variable in hot paths and a single reference plus a message handoff for worker-shared state.
